20 The graph shows the relationship between stress and strain for three wires of the same linear
dimensions but made from different materials.
P
stress
Q
R
0.1
0
0
1.0
strain
Which statements are correct?
1
The extension of P is approximately twice that of Q for the same stress.
2
The ratio of the Young modulus for P to that of Q is approximately two.
3
For strain less than 0.1, R obeys Hooke’s law.
A
1, 2 and 3
B
1 and 3 only
C
2 and 3 only
D
2 only

hints: Look at a horizontal line of constant stress on the P and Q graphs and compare their strain values on the horizontal axis.
Recall that Young modulus $E = \text{stress} / \text{strain}$, so $E$ is the gradient of a stress against strain graph.
Check the shape of curve R from the origin to strain 0.1 and recall the graph shape for Hooke's law.
walkthrough: The wires have the same original length and area, so strain is proportional to extension and stress is proportional to force. Comparing strains at the same stress is the same as comparing extensions.
For the same vertical stress value, line P is to the left of line Q, with about half the strain. So extension of P is about half that of Q, making statement 1 false.

Young modulus is $E = \frac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}}$, the gradient of the stress-strain graph. The initial gradient of P is approximately twice the gradient of Q, so $E_P / E_Q$ is approximately two and statement 2 is true.

Hooke's law requires stress proportional to strain, which is a straight line through the origin. Curve R is approximately straight from strain 0 to about 0.1 before it flattens, so statement 3 is true.
Only statements 2 and 3 are correct. This is option C.

A.explanation: Statement 1 is false, so any combination including 1 is wrong. P has the smaller strain for a given stress.

B.explanation: Statement 1 is false because P is steeper than Q, so its extension is about half, not twice, that of Q at the same stress.

C.explanation: Statements 2 and 3 are true. The gradient for P is about twice that for Q, and R is initially straight up to strain 0.1.

D.explanation: Statement 2 alone is incomplete because statement 3 is also true. R shows a linear stress-strain section for strain less than 0.1.
